title: Married at the Table
subtitle: Five sessions for a husband and wife who want to disciple each other, not just coexist
summary: Most couples share a bed, a budget, and a calendar, and never once share the deepest thing. They coexist. They are kind, they are tired, they are busy, and the years go by without either of them ever helping the other come nearer to God on purpose. This study is five sessions for the two of you at your own table. It begins with the person you promised your life to being the first and closest person you will ever disciple. It moves through praying out loud together, reading the Word together as heirs of the same grace, practicing confession and forgiveness where it is hardest to practice, and finally a love that serves instead of a love that rules. Leadership here is never a power hierarchy. It is two people washing feet, turning toward God together and toward each other honestly.
setting: Your own table, the two of you, phones away. The most important small group either of you will ever be in.
forWho: A married couple who want their marriage to be a place where both of them grow toward God, and the engaged couple preparing for it.
rhythm: Five sessions, just the two of you, over a meal or after the kids are down, unhurried and honest.
leaderNote: The couple is each other's first and closest disciple, and most couples have never once thought of the marriage that way. Keep the tone mutual and gentle. This is not one spouse fixing the other. It is two people turning toward God together, and toward each other honestly. There is no leader in this room and no student. If one of you carries this study and the other follows, you have already missed it. Sit level. Answer your own questions before you wait on your spouse to answer theirs. The goal of every session is not to win a point but to be a little more known and a little more helped by the person across the table.

sessions.title: The First Person You Disciple Is the One You Married
sessions.bigIdea: Two become one flesh, which means your spouse is not a roommate you are managing but a self you are now bound to. And the model for a husband's love is not a boss but a Savior who gave himself up. To disciple your spouse is simply to want them near to God, and to spend yourself so they get there.
sessions.open: When you married, what did you think the marriage was mainly for? Say it honestly, even if the honest answer is company, or kids, or just not being alone.
sessions.read: Read Genesis 2:24 out loud. Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. Then read Ephesians 5:25-33. Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word. In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church. Let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
observe: The pattern for a husband's love is Christ giving himself up. What does that make the love cost, and who pays it?
Paul says the aim is that he might sanctify her, might help her grow holy. What is the love actually for, beyond feeling good?
talk: One flesh means your spouse's growth toward God is now your own concern, not their private project. Where have the two of you been living as two separate believers under one roof instead of one flesh helping each other toward God?

Christ loved by giving himself up, not by taking charge. Where has love in this marriage quietly become about getting what I want, and where has it looked like laying myself down? Each of you answer for yourself, not for the other.

To want your spouse near to God is the plainest form of love there is. Ask each other out loud, without flinching: what is one thing I do that helps you toward God, and one thing I do that gets in the way?
sessions.practice: This week, each of you name one concrete way you will spend yourself for the other's good with no return expected, an hour taken off their plate, a burden carried, a task done without being asked. Do it quietly. Watch what it does to the room.
sessions.send: You did not marry a project to fix. You married a person to help home. Start spending yourself for that.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other couple you trust that you are doing this study, and ask them the question you just asked each other, what helps you toward God and what gets in the way. A marriage that talks about this makes it normal for the next one to.

sessions.title: Praying as Two, Not Alone
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus said that where two agree and gather in his name, he is there among them. The two he had in mind can be the two of you. Praying out loud together is the most exposed thing most couples never do, and the most joining thing they could.
sessions.open: Growing up, did you ever hear two people pray out loud together, not at church but in a kitchen or a bedroom? What did it sound like, or was it simply absent?
sessions.read: Read Matthew 18:19-20 out loud. Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them. Notice the smallest number Jesus names is two. Not a crowd, not a congregation. Two people who agree, with him in the middle.
observe: What is the smallest gathering Jesus promises to be present in? Who could those two people be in your house?
The two agree, and then they ask. What comes before the asking, and why might agreeing out loud be the hard part?
talk: Many couples will share a bank account, a body, and a mortgage, and still never pray a sentence out loud together, because it feels more naked than any of those. Is that true of us? If it is, name what makes it feel exposed, fumbling for words, being heard, not knowing how to start.

Jesus puts himself between the two who gather. What might change in how we handle a hard week, a fear about money, a worry about a child, if we brought it to him together instead of each carrying it alone?

Try it right now, before the nerve fades. Each of you say one short sentence to God out loud, a thank you or a please, with the other listening. That was praying as two. What was it like to be heard by your spouse while talking to God?
sessions.practice: Pray together out loud once a day this week, even for thirty seconds, even one sentence each. Hold hands if it helps. Do not grade it and do not fix each other's words. The aim is not eloquence. The aim is that you stop praying about each other only alone.
sessions.send: The two of you agreeing in prayer is a gathering Jesus promised to attend. Stop leaving him waiting for a crowd.
sessions.passItOn: Ask an older couple whose marriage you respect whether they pray together, and how they started, and what got them past the awkward beginning. Then tell a younger or newer couple that you have begun. A habit this quiet spreads only when someone admits they do it.

sessions.title: The Word Between You
sessions.bigIdea: Peter tells husbands to live with their wives as heirs together of the grace of life, and Paul tells the whole household to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly. Scripture was never meant to sit on a shelf between the two of you. It was meant to be the thing you read, argue with, and are shaped by together, as equal heirs of the same grace.
sessions.open: When was the last time the two of you read anything together, out loud, all the way through? A verse, a chapter, anything. Be honest if the answer is never.
sessions.read: Read 1 Peter 3:7 out loud. Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered. Then read Colossians 3:16. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
observe: Peter calls the wife an heir with the husband of the same grace. What does the word together do to any idea of one spouse ranking over the other?
Peter warns that treating a spouse wrongly can get in the way of your prayers. What does that say about how tied the marriage and the faith really are?
talk: Heirs together of the grace of life. Not a teacher and a pupil, not a head office and a branch, but two people who inherited the same thing. Where in our marriage have we let one of us become the spiritual one and the other the passenger? What did that cost the passenger, and what did it cost the one carrying it alone?

Colossians says the word of Christ should dwell in us richly and that we should teach and admonish one another. One another. That means each of you gets to speak into the other. When did you last let your spouse correct you from Scripture, and how did you take it?

Reading the Bible together will feel clumsy at first, and one of you may know it better than the other. How do we keep the more familiar one from lecturing and the less familiar one from checking out, so that it stays two heirs at one table?
sessions.practice: Pick one short passage and read it together three times this week, out loud, taking turns. After each reading, each of you says one plain thing, something you noticed or something it asked of you. No commentary needed, no right answer, just the word between you and both of you talking back to it.
sessions.send: You are not a teacher and a student. You are two heirs of one grace. Read like it.
sessions.passItOn: Hand your short passage to another couple and ask them to read it the same way, three times, one thought each. Tell them what surprised you. Two couples reading the same few verses gives you something real to talk about the next time you are together.

sessions.title: Confession and Forgiveness at Home
sessions.bigIdea: Paul says do not let the sun go down on your anger, and James says confess your sins to one another that you may be healed. The marriage is the first place we ever practice the gospel on a real person. If forgiveness is not real at your table, it is not yet real anywhere.
sessions.open: In the home you grew up in, how were fights handled? Did anyone ever say the words I was wrong, or did things just go quiet until they blew over?
sessions.read: Read Ephesians 4:26-32 out loud. Be angry and do not sin, do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil. Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. Then read James 5:16. Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.
observe: Paul does not say never be angry. He gives anger a curfew, before the sun goes down. Why might a deadline matter more than the feeling itself?
James ties confession to healing. What does that suggest about the unconfessed things a couple carries for years?
talk: The gospel says we forgive as God in Christ forgave us, freely, at cost, without making the other earn it back. Where in this marriage are we still making the other earn back something we claim to have forgiven? Each of you answer for a place you are guarding, not a place you are owed.

Do not let the sun go down on your anger is not about faking peace by bedtime. It is about refusing to let a wall get built brick by silent brick. What is our pattern when we are hurt, going cold, going loud, going away? What would it take to break it before the sun goes down?

Confession is harder than forgiveness because it costs you the story where you were mostly right. Is there something one of you needs to actually name to the other, plainly, tonight, with no but attached? If you are ready, say it now, and let the other receive it before answering.
sessions.practice: This week, the first time either of you is wrong, say the two hardest words in a marriage, I was wrong, with no explanation trailing behind them. And the one receiving it practices the reply of the gospel, plainly, I forgive you. Small offenses are the training ground for the large ones.
sessions.send: Your table is the first place the gospel gets real or stays theory. Let the sun go down on the anger, not on the marriage.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one other married couple the plainest true thing here, that the marriage is where we first practice the gospel on a real person. You do not have to hand over your fights. Just hand over the sentence. It preaches on its own.

sessions.title: Serving, Not Lording
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus said the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you, and whoever would be great must become a servant. Paul puts the whole marriage under one command, submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. Leadership in a Christian marriage is not a chain of command. It is a competition to serve.
sessions.open: When you hear the words leadership in marriage, what picture comes to mind first, honestly? Where do you think that picture came from?
sessions.read: Read Mark 10:42-45 out loud. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Then read Ephesians 5:21. Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
observe: Jesus names how the world's leaders operate, lording it over, and then says it shall not be so among you. What exactly is he forbidding, and what is he putting in its place?
Ephesians 5:21 comes right before the famous verses about husbands and wives. How does starting with submit to one another change how everything after it reads?
talk: Jesus draws a hard line between the way the Gentiles lead, by power over people, and the way it shall be among his own, by service under them. Where has authority in this marriage, from either of us, looked more like the Gentiles than like Jesus? Name your own version of lording it, not your spouse's.

Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ puts both of you low, both of you serving. That is not weakness and it is not one of you losing. What would it look like this week for the two of you to compete over who gets to serve rather than over who gets their way?

The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life. That is the only leadership Jesus ever modeled. If that were the pattern in our home, what is one thing that would have to change, and which of us needs to move first? The honest answer is usually both, starting with me.
sessions.practice: This week, each of you find one thing your spouse dreads or dislikes doing, and do it for them without being asked and without keeping score. Then, harder, let the other serve you without deflecting it or paying it back. Learn to receive service as well as give it. That, too, is submitting to one another.
sessions.send: In this house it shall not be like the Gentiles. The one who leads is the one who kneels. Go compete over who gets to serve.
sessions.passItOn: This is the last session, so send the whole thing on. Invite another couple to their own table for these five weeks, and tell them the plain truth, that the first person you disciple is the one you married, and almost no one ever taught you how. Then point them toward the help that is here.
